about: Grobin (Grobiņa in Kurland, taken to be Rimbert's Seeburg), one market, written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/grobin.md. A draft for the user to overwrite. Every person here is invented: no king, chief, merchant or craftsman of this place is named in any text, and no Curonian at all before 1230. No Curonian god, rite or word is put in anyone's mouth, and no mark on the water is named, because none is known. The table (ports_793.json) closes the port in 850 and the chronicle burns it about 854: the sites here run to 854, and the ships to 850 as the unlock table has them. (?) = not checked on a page that was opened.

ports.summary: A fort hill on a spit of a small river, a black-earthed settlement beside it and three fields of the dead round both: Gotlanders and Svear have lived here among the Curonians for five generations, and nobody can say any longer whose place it is. A merchant comes for amber after the gales, grey squirrel in spring, seal oil, wax and honey, and brings iron, blades, beads and salt; everything goes by weight, since no coin is struck on this coast. He gets in over a sand bar and across a wide shallow lake, and he gets out again only if the wind and the bar allow.
ports.seasons: The sea is shut by ice from the first hard frost to well after the spring thaw, and the ice goes out late here. The Gotlanders come when it opens, wanting furs; the gales of autumn throw amber on the open shore, and the last ship must be over the bar before the lake skins over.

history.text: People from Gotland and from the Mälar valley settle beside a Curonian fort on the river Ālande, about 11 km in from the open coast. The place is older than Hedeby and Birka both.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' ('comparable in many ways to Hedeby and Birka but probably predating them both'); lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; dossier 1, 5

history.text: A flat stone carved with two duck-like birds, of a kind otherwise made only on Gotland, is set in a grave in the mound field. It is 0.70 m high.
history.source: en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis' (found 1987 at Priediens; second half of the 7th century); dossier 2, 7

history.text: The settlement stands: a fort plateau up to 80 m by 45 m, about 3 ha of houses on black earth, and grave fields of some thousands of burials. Nothing is recorded for the year, and no ruler is named.

By the Latvian accounts the Curonians take the settlement over about now. The Northmen's graves are dated to 800 by one page and to 850 by others: between those years the Gotlanders and Svear stop being buried here.
history.source: lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' and 'Grobiņas pilskalns'; en.wikipedia, de.wikipedia and sv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' (the pages disagree (?)); dossier 5, 8

history.text: The Cori, who 'had in former time been in subjection to the Swedes', have 'a long while since rebelled'. Their kingdom holds five towns.
history.source: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 30 (tr. C. H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North, 1921). The year stands for 'before about 853': Rimbert gives none.

history.text: This year a fleet of the Danes came to plunder the Cori and bring them under. The men of the five towns gathered, killed half the Danes, and took half their ships, with gold, silver and spoils.
history.source: Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921); the year is about 853 (?)

history.text: This year Olof, king of the Svear, 'collected an immense army' and came first to a town of the Cori called Seeburg, which they 'ravaged and despoiled and burnt'. Then they marched five days to Apulia and besieged it eight days.
history.source: Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921); chronicle_793.json 854-courland-war. Seeburg is taken to be this place: a scholar's match, made after the digs of 1929, not a fact in the text. sv.wikipedia gives 855 (?)

history.text: On the ninth day at Apulia the Cori offered the gold and arms taken from the Danes, 'half-a-pound of silver for each individual man now in this town', the old tribute and thirty hostages. The Svear took it and went home.
history.source: Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921). The project reckons half a pound at 120 d a man (economy/furs_amber_ivory_slaves.md)

history.text: After the burning the market loses its standing to others, such as Truso. No later graves of Northmen are found. The Curonians keep the fort hill, and its layer of use runs on for four hundred years.
history.source: de.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis' (culture layer 5th to 13th century); dossier 5

history.text: A saga written three hundred years later sets a truce of half a month for trading in Kurland, and a raid when it ran out. No place is named.
history.source: Egil's saga c. 46 (13th century; LATER; the year is a guess (?)); en.wikipedia 'Courland'; dossier 3, 7

eras.text: A mixed place with no one lord. Gotland households trade on the black earth and bury their women in island dress; a few armed men from the Mälar valley keep the fort hill and still speak of a tribute their fathers took; the Curonians, who were here first, sell them amber, pelts and wax and are more of them every year. Three tongues in the market, and every bargain weighed twice.

The Curonians hold the hill. Whether the Northmen were bought out, married in or pushed off depends on who tells it, and on what the house did here. The Gotland booths thin to two or three; the mound field is no longer added to. Ships from Gotland still come in spring, and are counted as guests now, by the day.

War on this shore. About 853 the five towns break a Danish fleet and the market is suddenly full of Danish gold and Danish ships for sale. The next summer the Svear come with their king. A merchant who is here at the wrong moon sees the town burn; one who is here just before it can do something about who is inside.

No market for strangers. The settlement is ash under new grass and the three fields of the dead are pasture; the Curonians keep the fort and pay the Svear a tribute for as long as the Svear can come and fetch it. A ship that stands in to this coast in these years is taken for a raider or is one. What trade there is goes by a truce counted in days.

sites.name: The bar and the open shore
sites.see: A long low coast of pale sand with surf standing on it and no haven anywhere: dunes, bent grass, a line of dark pine behind. In one place the surf is broken and brown water runs out through it over a bar. A flat-bottomed boat lies there with a man standing in it, holding a sounding pole. Wind, gulls, and in autumn people walking the tide line with baskets, heads down.
sites.source: A harbourless surf coast, a sand bar, and an outlet from the lake that kept silting shut until a canal was dug in 1697-1703 (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md; dossier 1). Where the outlet lay in 793 and how deep it was are not known, so nothing here is named or measured (?). Amber gathered after the autumn gales is the region's pattern, not this place's evidence (trade_year_793.json curonia; dossier 4). The pilot and the porters who drag a boat over are invented.

sites.name: The reed lake
sites.see: A wide sheet of shallow grey-brown water behind the dunes, so shallow that the pole touches almost everywhere. Reed beds stand out from both shores and round low islands; fish traps of withy show in rows. Far across, a thread of smoke marks where the river comes in. Coots, the knock of a paddle on a logboat, the smell of mud and cut reed.
sites.source: Lake Liepāja: 37 km2, 16 km long, 2 m deep on average and 3 m at most, 13 islands, behind a sand bar (en.wikipedia 'Lake Liepāja'); 'the lake served as a harbour' (de.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'); dossier 1. The traps and the fishers are invented in the period's manner; no fishery is recorded.

sites.name: The bank under the hill
sites.see: A bend of a small slow river, alder and willow on the far side, and on the near side a trodden bank of dark earth where boats lie nose-in: two riveted boats of the Gotlanders, a pegged boat of the coast, a row of logboats. Above them the fort hill rises steep on its spit with a timber fence along the top. Wood smoke, tar, wet dogs, and three tongues being shouted at once.
sites.source: The fort stands on a spit on the right bank of the Ālande, which guarded it on three sides (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'; en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'). The landing is 'riverbank' in ports_793.json; no jetty has been reported (dossier 1, 2). How far a laden boat could come up the river is not known (?). No toll is recorded and none is taken here.

sites.name: The black earth
sites.see: Low timber houses and open-fronted booths on ground so dark with old hearths that it stains the shoes. In front, a plank on two trestles with a folding balance on it, a heap of rough amber the colour of honey and dirty wax, bundles of grey pelts tied by the forty. Behind, the hill. A woman in island dress, two brooches and a string of beads, is counting something a second time.
sites.source: The settlement of about 3 ha beside the fort, culture layer up to 0.6 m: Nerman's 'black earth' (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'; sv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'). Goods as the region's pattern: amber, squirrel, seal oil, wax, honey, captives out; swords, iron tools, glass beads, salt in (goods_793.json; trade_year_793.json curonia; dossier 4). Silver by weight, no coin (dossier 4) (?). The spine's hook: amber weighed against silver (silver_road).

sites.name: The Gotlanders' store
sites.see: A squat log house with a turf roof and the only door in the settlement that has an iron lock. Inside it is dark and dry: sacks of amber sorted by size, pelts hung from the rafters out of reach of mice, a stack of bar iron with a hide over it, a tub of seal oil that can be smelt from the door. A tally of notched sticks hangs on a peg by the post.
sites.source: invented in the period's manner: no storehouse has been reported (dossier 2, 'not found'). Goods kept over a winter for the spring ships are what a settlement of traders 'comparable to Staraya Ladoga' (de.wikipedia 'Grobiņa') would need (?).

sites.name: The gate of the fort
sites.see: A steep path up the spit to a gap in a fence of upright logs, with an earth bank as high as a man across the one side the river does not guard. Two men sit in the gap with spears across their knees and a board game between them. From up here the whole place shows: the bend of the river, the booths, and in a half circle beyond them the low humps of the dead.
sites.source: The fort plateau up to 80 by 40-45 m with a rampart at the east end about 30 m wide and 2 m high, in use from the 5th to the 13th century (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'; dossier 2). Which people held it in 793 is not settled: the game puts a few Svear at the gate until 800 and Curonians after (?). No hall and no ruler are named, so there is no audience here. The board game: town_games_793.json lists grobin.

sites.name: The field of the armed men
sites.see: A wide heath of low round mounds, each a few paces across and no higher than a man's knee, hundreds of them, running off among birch and pine. The oldest are furred with heather; the newest is bare sand with a burnt patch beside it. In the grass between two old ones stands a thin flat stone, grey, with two birds cut on it. Wind in the pines, and nobody about.
sites.source: The Priediens field: low mounds mostly 7 to 10 m across and 0.5 m high, cremations, men with Scandinavian weapons; about 2,000 by one count and about 1,000 by another (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'; sv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa': the counts disagree). The picture stone was found in a grave here in 1987; that it once stood in the open is the game's guess (?). That this is the field of the Mälar men is from memory of Nerman (?).

sites.name: The women's ground
sites.see: A level stretch of sandy turf by a stand of old hornbeams, with nothing on it but small ringed patches where the grass grows greener. No mounds, no stones. A woman kneels at one of the patches, pouring something from a cup, and the brooches on her dress are the kind worn on one island in the whole sea. A lark, and the settlement's smoke beyond the trees.
sites.source: The Smukumi flat-grave field: more than 100 graves dug, women with Scandinavian brooches, pendants, rings and glass beads, men with swords and shield bosses; cremations (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'). Women in the flat graves wear Gotland's belt buckles and brooches (en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'). The hornbeams are from the Latvian derivation of the name (gruobīns, a hornbeam wood) (?). The offering poured is invented.

sites.name: Rodlikn's long house
sites.see: The longest house on the black earth: a hearth down the middle, sleeping benches along both walls with sheepskins on them, a loom by the door where the light is, and a brewing vat under the eaves. A board for the table game hangs on a peg with its pieces in a bag. It smells of malt, smoke and drying fish. Every bench has a name, and one of them is kept for your crew after the first night.
sites.source: invented. The Gotland women of the flat graves (en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; de.wikipedia 'Grobiņa') are the nearest thing to named households the place has; that one of them lodged strangers and brewed is the game's guess (?). After 818 the house is kept by whoever the story 'Two birds on a stone' left in it.

sites.name: The house of the woman who is asked
sites.see: A small round-cornered house at the edge of the hornbeams, apart from the rest, with bunches of dry plants hanging under the eaves and a fire that is never let out. An old woman sits on the threshold with her hands in her lap. People come to the fence, wait to be looked at, and say what they want to know. She does not get up for Northmen, and does not send them away either.
sites.source: Adam of Bremen, about 1075, says the Curonians' houses are 'full of pagan soothsayers, diviners and necromancers' (en.wikipedia 'Curonians'; peoples/baltic_east.md): late for these years, and used lightly. What she does, whom she calls on and in what words is not recorded and is not written here: the player sees a question asked and an answer given, no more (?).

sites.name: The boat bank
sites.see: A level shelf of the river bank upstream of the landing, deep in chips. A boat of the coast stands half planked on blocks: broad, shallow, ten paces long, her strakes overlapping. Beside her a log as thick as a barrel is being hollowed with fire and adze by two men who do not look up. Split oak, a tar pot on a tripod, the tick of a mallet on wedges.
sites.source: ship_classes_793.json and story/ships_793.json: baltic_coastal_boat 'built_at' reric, truso, grobin ('riveted boats at Truso and Grobina'), and the logboat of the Balts (peoples/baltic_east.md 6). No yard, wright or slip has been found or named here (dossier 2, 3), so no person is placed at it: the work is done by men of both peoples who are paid by the day.

people.name: Botgair
people.trait: The oldest of the Gotland traders on the black earth, born here like his father. Patient, exact, and fonder of this place than of the island he calls home and has seen four times.
people.want: To stay. A bargain between the hill and the booths that lets his grandchildren be buried in the women's ground beside his mother.
people.fear: A spring when the Curonians bring their amber to the bank, look at his scale, and carry it on past him to a Gotland ship.
people.voice: Slow and level. Weighs first and talks after. Calls Gotland 'the island' and this place 'here', and says 'we' for both without noticing.
people.looks: Near fifty, lean, grey-fair beard in a single plait, a brown wool tunic to the knee with a tablet-woven hem, a Gotland belt buckle of bronze, a folding balance in a wooden case hung at his hip.
knows: what amber, squirrel, wax and seal oil stand at today, in cut silver by weight, and what they stood at last spring
which Gotland ships came in this year, whose they are, and what they carried home
how much iron and how many blades the hill wants, and how much it can pay for
the way silver comes to Gotland from the east, at second hand: he has never been past the island

ties.note: his brother's widow; he keeps the store and she keeps the house, and each reckons the other's accounts in private
thirty years of bargains across one plank; they have never eaten in each other's houses
the Svea on the hill talks of tribute; Botgair thinks the word alone will cost the booths their trade
pays him in salt each spring for bringing the Gotland ships over the bar, and is a spring behind
a cousin's son on the island who brings iron, takes the amber home, and sleeps at this fire on his way east
the Dane's sister is married to Botgair's son; the two men have traded amber prices through her for years (?)
the Birka man buys furs here in a good year and counts Botgair's forty-bundles over again in front of him
wax for iron by way of a third man's ship; each keeps a notched stick with the other's name on it
showed the go-between's boy the folding scale, and has been weighed on it by him ever since
the woman who speaks for the trappers on the eastern river has learned to ask where his amber was last offered

lines.greet: A Frisian. I have heard of you and not seen one. Put your silver on the pan and we will find out how far you came.
lines.greet_again: You are back, and the bar let you in again. Good. I kept the large pieces by. Sit. Weigh first, then tell me the news.
rumour: The Svea on the hill says the Curonians owe tribute. His grandfather took it. He has eleven men. I have counted them more often than he has.
White silver with writing all round came to the island last year. My cousin's son had six pieces. He would not say what he gave for them.
Amber is cheap after the gales and dear at midsummer. Everybody knows it. The ice knows it too, and that is why it stays cheap.
A Birka man counted my pelts twice and found forty both times. He seemed sorry about it.
lines.saying: Weigh it when you buy and weigh it when you sell. What happens to it between is your own affair.
lines.farewell: Go out on the morning wind, not the evening one. And if you see the island, tell it we are still here.

people.source: invented. Gotlanders living and buried here are from the grave fields (de.wikipedia and en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; dossier 1, 3); no trader of the place is named. Name: Bót- + -gair, both on the later rune stones of Gotland (names_placeholder.json) (?).

people.name: Rodlikn
people.trait: A Gotland widow who keeps the long house where strangers sleep. Remembers every crew by where they sat, what they drank and what they left unpaid, and holds none of it against them.
people.want: A stone with two birds on it for her own grave, cut on the island as her husband's people once had one cut, before nobody is left who knows why.
people.fear: That she will be the last woman laid in the women's ground in island dress, with no daughter to pin the brooches.
people.voice: Quick and warm, with an edge. Asks after each of your crew by the bench he slept on. Counts cups aloud while she pours.
people.looks: About forty, small and straight, fair hair under a linen cloth, a dark wool dress held by two animal-head brooches of Gotland make with a string of glass beads between, a box brooch at the throat, keys and a small knife on a chain.
knows: who is in the settlement tonight, what ship they came by, and whether they paid
what the Gotland ships will want in spring, before they know it themselves
who is buried where in the women's ground, six mothers back
which of the hill's men can be trusted in drink, and which of your own

ties.note: her dead husband's brother; she feeds his guests and he forgets to reckon her malt
the old Curonian woman cured her fever twice and was paid in beads; they have forty words in common and use all of them
he has slept on her end bench every storm night since he was a boy
his men drink on the word 'tribute' and she has stopped pouring for it
her mother's kin on the island, three generations off; she knows their farm's name and has never seen it
Ravn slept here once, years back, on a ship out of the west; she remembers the bench and that he set her a riddle she has not yet answered

lines.greet: Four men and a small boat. You came over the bar in that? Then you have earned the bench by the fire. Ale first. Names when you are dry.
lines.greet_again: Your bench is kept. The steersman's too, by the wall, where he likes it. One of you owes me for a cup. I forget which.
rumour: My mother wore these brooches and her mother before. Nobody here can cast the like. When they break I shall have to become a Curonian.
A stone with two birds stands in the men's field. My husband's people put it there. Which birds? Water birds. That is all anyone knows.
The pilot will not take silver for the bar from a man who sleeps here. Do not tell him I said so. He likes to be asked.
Your old Northman set me a riddle before you were a merchant. Tell him I am still thinking, and that it is ill-mannered to live so long.
lines.saying: A guest is counted by cups, a friend by winters.
lines.farewell: Go well. I will turn your bench to the wall so that nobody else warms it. Come before the ice or not until after.

people.source: invented. Women in the flat graves wear Gotland's own brooches and buckles (en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'); the animal-head and box brooches are Gotland's kinds (from memory (?)). No woman of the place is named. Name: Hróð- + -líkn, both on Gotland's stones (the Ardre stones; names_placeholder.json) (?).

people.name: Arnvald
people.trait: The head of the few armed Svear who still sit on the fort hill, as their fathers did. Proud, bored, and honest enough to know that eleven men are not a lordship.
people.want: Blades. Enough good Frankish swords to make the old tribute worth asking for again, or else a way home with his name whole.
people.fear: To be the man in whose time the hill was given up, and to have it told at Uppsalir by people who were never here.
people.voice: Short and flat. Says less than he means. Speaks of his father's day as if it were last year, and of next year not at all.
people.looks: Mid-thirties, broad, red-brown beard cut square, a grey wool tunic and wide trousers bound at the calf, a single-edged long knife in a worn scabbard across the belly, a shield with an iron boss leaning by him.
knows: how many men each of the five towns of the Cori could bring to a field, by his own reckoning
what a tribute was in his grandfather's day: so many pelts a hearth, and who collected it
what a sword fetches here, and that the Franks' king forbids their sale
who at Birka and Uppsalir still speaks for the men on this hill, and who has forgotten them

ties.note: they want the same blades and both know it; they are civil, and each has a man watching the other's door
thinks the Gotlander would sell the hill for a good amber year
eleven men's ale since midsummer, and an apology he has not made
a man at the kings' mounds who still tells of the men who took tribute over the sea; Arnvald sends him a pelt each year so that he goes on telling it
Holmfast carries his messages to the bay for nothing, and is the only man who brings an answer
was promised blades by a Frisian of that name through a Dane; he has paid in pelts and seen no swords
sent a man to ask her whether the tribute would be paid again, and got the man back with a remedy for wind

lines.greet: A trader from the Franks' river. You will have iron, then. I do not ask what kind. Sit down where the others cannot hear you.
lines.greet_again: You again. Good. The hill is still ours, as you see. Count the men at the gate if you like. I do, every morning.
rumour: My father's father took a pelt from every hearth between here and the amber shore. I take what the Gotlander's guests leave in the cup.
The Curonian go-between asked the price of a sword last moon. He asked it of me. That is either manners or a warning.
A Frisian promised me blades through a Dane two summers ago. I have the Dane's word and the Frisian's name. Neither cuts.
lines.saying: A man with a spear is asked his price. A man with a sword is told it.
lines.farewell: Go safely. If you speak of this hill at Birka, say it is held. Do not say by how many.

people.source: invented. One of the three grave fields is 'military in character', with men of the Mälar valley under low mounds with their weapons (en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'); the Cori 'had in former time been in subjection to the Swedes, but had a long while since rebelled' (Rimbert c. 30, Robinson 1921). That a few Svear still sat on the fort in 793 is the game's reading of an open question (dossier 8) (?); he is no ruler and is called none. Name: Arn- + -vald, both on the Uppland stones.

people.name: Kantegede
people.trait: The Curonian who stands between the hill forts inland and the strangers' booths: three tongues, a long memory, and a habit of agreeing with the last speaker until the weighing starts.
people.want: Iron and blades for his own people, at a price set by them and not by the men on the hill. And his son standing where he stands.
people.fear: A quarrel over one word, tribute, that ends with the booths burnt and no Gotland ship coming in spring with salt.
people.voice: Courteous and roundabout in the Northmen's tongue, which he speaks well and slowly. Never says no. Says 'it may be' and lets you learn what that means.
people.looks: About forty-five, tall, clean chin and long fair moustache, a pale undyed wool tunic with a bronze neck ring and a spiral arm ring, a staff notched along one side, soft hide shoes.
knows: what the forts inland will bring down this season: amber, pelts, wax, honey, and after a fight, people
what each of them wants for it, which is seldom silver
the word a Curonian uses when he means the bargain is off
how the five towns stand toward each other this year, in outline; the rest he keeps

ties.note: his son, whom he is teaching the Northmen's tongue and the folding scale, in that order
thirty years across one plank; he would be sorry to see the Gotlander go, and has said so to nobody
greets him each morning by name and counts his men each evening
his mother's sister; he does nothing large without asking her, and does not always like the answer
the lord of the Este's fort says men of this coast raid his amber shore by boat; Kantegede answers that he speaks for traders, and that nobody speaks for the others
the Wend sends honey prices up the coast by any ship; Kantegede sends back the price of pelts, a little raised

lines.greet: You are welcome here, stranger. You come from far. It may be we have what you want. It may be you have what we want. Let us sit.
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the small boat. My son said you would come back. He has been practising your numbers. He is not yet good.
rumour: Silver is a fine thing. You cannot plough with it. My people ask what else you carry, and they ask before they look at your scale.
The men on the hill speak of an old custom of gifts. We remember it also. We remember that it stopped.
At the lake of the Este they weigh amber by the sack and laugh at ours. Their sacks are small. I have this from a man who carried one.
lines.saying: The one who speaks both tongues is cheated in both.
lines.farewell: Go with a fair wind. When you come again, bring salt. It may be that it will be remembered.

people.source: invented. No Curonian of these years is named in any source (dossier 3, 8); a go-between is inferred from two peoples trading in one place, and he is no chief. Neck and arm rings of bronze as Baltic dress are from memory (?). Name: two Old Prussian stems of the later records (Kante- and -gede: names_placeholder.json) standing in, since no Curonian name survives before 1230 (?).

people.name: Wissegerde
people.trait: Kantegede's son, a boy at the plank in 793 and the man who runs the market for the Curonians once the hill is theirs. Sharper than his father and less polite; he learned to count from strangers and has not forgiven them for it.
people.want: The market kept open on Curonian terms: guests by the day, a gift at the gate, and no word ever again about what was owed to whose grandfather.
people.fear: Sails in a number he cannot count from the dunes. He has been told since he was small that the Svear will come back.
people.voice: Fast, plain, and impatient with roundabout talk. Names a price and waits. Laughs once, loudly, when something is true.
people.looks: A young man in 800 and grey by 850: tall like his father, fair hair tied back, a blue-dyed tunic with a bronze neck ring, a folding balance of the Northmen's kind at his belt and a spear never far off.
knows: every price on this shore, by weight, and what the same goods stood at when his father kept the plank
which Gotland and Birka skippers are still let in, and which were told not to come back
after 853: how many Danish ships lie on the lake shore and what the gold from them weighs
how many days' truce a stranger's gift at the gate buys this year

ties.note: his father, who taught him two tongues and told him to be courteous in both
the pilot let him hold the pole when he was eight; nobody crosses the bar without Wissegerde hearing of it
the Gotlander showed him the folding scale as a boy, and has been weighed on it ever since
the Birka man trades here by leave and asks too many questions about the old days
the Dane who weighs at the lake of the Este; they send each other false prices by every ship and both know the true ones

lines.greet: A gift at the gate, then the plank. That is the custom now. Your father's house may have known another. This is the one that holds.
lines.greet_again: I know your boat. My father knew your house. Lay the gift down and never mind the speech. What do you carry?
rumour: The Danes came with many ships and went home with half. We have the other half on the lake shore. Do you want to buy a ship?
There is gold in the market this year, with crosses on some of it. The Danes took it from someone. Now someone will come to take it from us.
My father never said no to a stranger. I say it twice a day. The amber is the same price.
A Birka man asks me how many we are inside the fence. I ask him how many oars his king has. Neither of us answers.
lines.saying: Count the guest's days aloud, so that he hears the last one coming.
lines.farewell: Go while the truce runs. Come again with salt and iron and you will find it has been counted afresh.

people.source: invented. That the Curonians take the place over between 800 and 850 is the Latvian pages' account (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; dossier 5); the Danes' defeat and the gold and ships taken from them are Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921). A truce counted in days is the saga's picture of a Kurland market (Egil's saga c. 46; LATER; peoples/baltic_east.md). He dies in the burning unless the house got him out (the story 'The gods who would not answer'). Name: Wisse- and -gerde, Old Prussian stems of the later records standing in (?).

people.name: Tulegaud
people.trait: The Curonian who takes ships over the bar and across the lake. Cheerful, incurious about cargoes, and never wrong about water he has poled that morning.
people.want: To be asked. Then salt, a good knife, and a boat's company that does what he says the first time.
people.fear: A winter storm that moves the outlet while he sleeps, and a Gotland ship that trusts last year's channel.
people.voice: Few words in the Northmen's tongue and all of them about depth, wind and bottom. Points more than he speaks. Laughs at laden boats.
people.looks: Under thirty, wiry and burnt brown, fair hair cropped with a knife, a short sleeveless hide coat over a wool shirt, bare legs wet to the thigh, a sounding pole twice his height marked in hand-spans.
knows: where the water runs out over the bar today, and where it ran last year: it is not the same place
how deep your boat sits, to the hand-span, after one look
how the lake lies in every wind, and where a boat can wait out a blow among the reeds
who came in before you this season and how low in the water they went out

ties.note: her end bench is his on storm nights; he brings her eels and takes no silver from her guests
the Gotlander owes him a spring's salt, and he has not asked for it, which worries the Gotlander more
taught the boy the pole and the lake; the boy now tells him who may come in
asks her before the first crossing of every spring, and has never said what she tells him
a Gotland skipper he has brought in eleven springs running; they share no tongue and get on well
the pilot of the Este's lake in his day; each has heard the other called the best on this sea, from skippers who wanted a lower fee

lines.greet: Small boat. Good. Deep? No. Good. You follow my pole, not your eyes. Your eyes are for another sea.
lines.greet_again: The small boat. I saw your sail and knew the mast. The water has moved since you were here. Follow me again.
rumour: A Gotlander came in on his own last spring, by the old way. We dug him out with spades. He paid double and said nothing.
Three ships out this moon, all low. Furs do not sit a ship so low. I do not ask.
The lake skins over in one night. I have walked home across water I poled that morning.
lines.saying: Last year's channel drowns this year's fool.
lines.farewell: Out on the morning wind. I go ahead. When my pole goes up, you row. When I shout, you row harder.

people.source: invented. The outlet from the lake kept silting shut and shifting until the canal of 1697-1703 (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md; dossier 1): a place like that has a man who knows this morning's water. Where the outlet lay and how deep it was in 793 are unknown, and he names no mark (dossier 8). The flag unlock_pilot_curonia (the amber road chain) is his knowledge. Name: Tule- and -gaud, Old Prussian stems of the later records standing in (?).

people.name: Buite
people.trait: The old Curonian woman who is asked. Says little, sees who is lying, and treats a Northman's fever and a Curonian's the same, at the same price.
people.want: To be left to her fire and her plants, and to see her sister's son keep the peace between the hill and the booths until she is dead.
people.fear: Young men of either people who want an answer that tells them to do what they already mean to do.
people.voice: A handful of words in the Northmen's tongue, used exactly. Long silences that are not rude. Answers a question with what you should have asked.
people.looks: Near sixty, bent, white hair in two plaits under a wool cloth, a dark dress pinned at the shoulders with bronze pins joined by a chain, a string of rough amber, hands stained green and brown.
knows: which plants on this shore bring a fever down, close a wound or settle a stomach after bad water
what was asked of her this moon and by whom, which she does not tell
what the hill was like before any Svea was born who now sits on it, as her mother told it
whether a man at her fence means what he says

ties.note: her sister's son; he asks before every large bargain, and she tells him when he is being a coward
the Gotland woman brings beads and malt and sits without talking, which is rare in a stranger
he comes before the first crossing each spring; she tells him the same thing every year and he thinks it is new
he sent a man to ask whether the tribute would be paid again; she sent the man back with a remedy for wind
the woman who is asked at the lake of the Este; they send each other dried plants by the amber boats and have never met
they have never met and never will; a Frisian skipper once carried a bundle of dried root from one to the other, and a different root back

lines.greet: Sit. No, there, in the light. You came to ask a thing. First you ask the wrong thing. They all do. I will wait.
lines.greet_again: The one from the west river. Your man with the cough, he lives? Good. Then you owe me nothing, and you have come to ask again.
rumour: The Svea sent to ask if the gifts would come again. I sent him something for his belly. It was the truer answer.
The Gotland woman asks if her daughters' daughters will lie in her ground. I tell her to have daughters first.
Your people have one god, I hear, and he is jealous. Ours are many and they are busy. I do not know which is worse for a trader.
lines.saying: Ask before you go. Asking after is only weeping.
lines.farewell: Go. The water will take you out or it will not. That one I do not answer. Ask the man with the pole.

people.source: invented. Adam of Bremen, about 1075: the Curonians' houses are 'full of pagan soothsayers, diviners and necromancers' (en.wikipedia 'Curonians'; peoples/baltic_east.md 31): late, and used lightly. No god, rite or Curonian word is named, because none is recorded for these years (dossier 8). Pins joined by a chain as Baltic women's dress are from memory (?). Name: Buite, a Prussian woman's name of the 13th to 15th century records (peoples/baltic_east.md 7), standing in (?).

people.name: Vigfast
people.trait: A Birka fur trader who comes here by the Curonians' leave in the last years, and who has stood at the back of the priest's house at Birka often enough to be unsure which gods he owes.
people.want: The furs, and not to be standing on this bank when his own king's ships come round the dunes.
people.fear: That he will be asked, by one side or the other, how many men are inside the fence, and will answer.
people.voice: Careful, counts everything twice like his people, and drops his voice for anything about the king or the priest. Dates things by the Christians' fasts without noticing.
people.looks: About thirty-five, stocky, fair beard trimmed close, a good red-brown cloak with a ring pin of silver, wide trousers, a small hammer of iron on a thong at his neck and a cross of the same size beside it.
knows: what is said at Birka about this coast: who wants it raided and who wants it left to trade
what the priest at Birka teaches, roughly, and which of it he keeps
what squirrel and marten fetch at Birka against here, to the pennyweight
after the war: what was done at the fort five days inland, because he was there

ties.note: heard the bishop at Birka about 852 and took the sign of the cross, no more; keeps the fasts when he remembers
trades from a corner of the booth Holmfast's heir keeps at Birka, and pays for it in news of this coast
the old prefect's church was the first he stood in; he was at the burial
the Curonian lets him in by the day and counts the days aloud
the skald at old Grimulf's bench at Birka makes verses on whatever the king does; Vigfast tells him what truly happened and hears it come back larger

lines.greet: You are from the Franks' river. Then you are a Christian. Good. So am I, on fast days. Keep your voice down here about both.
lines.greet_again: Still trading on this bank? So am I. I count my days here now the way the Curonian counts them for me.
rumour: The Danes tried this coast and lost half their ships. At Birka the young men say: then we will do what Danes could not. Kings listen to that.
There is a bishop at Birka again, and the king let the lots be cast about him. They fell his way. I saw it.
We cast lots before the fort and found no god willing to help us. Not one. Have you ever stood among an army that has heard that?
Then some of us said, ask the Christians' god. It fell well. I have eaten no meat for forty days since, and I trade furs for a living.
lines.saying: Sacrifice to the old ones for the harvest. For a siege five days from the ships, ask whoever answers.
lines.farewell: Go before midsummer and do not come back this year. I cannot say more than that. I have said too much.

people.source: invented, to stand for the unnamed Svea merchants in Olof's host who 'had heard' Anskar and advised asking Christ, and for the vow kept afterwards: seven days at home, seven without meat, and after forty days another forty (Rimbert c. 30, Robinson 1921; dossier 3, 6). The lots at Birka about Anskar's coming: Rimbert c. 26-27 (?). His last two rumours are said only after the war, at Birka. The hammer worn beside a cross: BRIEF.md tone guide. Name: Víg- + -fast, both on the Uppland stones.

stories.title: Weighed twice
stories.summary: Amber is weighed against silver on one plank between two peoples who trust neither each other's scale nor each other's silver. A stranger who sleeps in neither camp is asked to hold the balance, and learns here, on a coast with no coin at all, what the white silver of the east is worth.
stories.picture: A plank on trestles on black ground under a fort hill: a lean Gotlander and a tall Curonian with a neck ring on either side of a folding balance, rough amber in one pan and cut silver in the other, and a Frisian merchant between them holding the beam level with one finger.

beats.text: Botgair weighs your pennies and gives you a number. Kantegede weighs them on a Curonian beam and gives you a smaller one. Each looks at you as if the other were not there.

Among Botgair's cut silver is a half coin, thin and white, with writing all round and no king's head. It came from the island, and to the island from the east. He will not sell it, but he lets you hold it (the thread's flag sv_first_dirham, if the house does not have it yet).
Dragomir the Wend has one like it on a thong. He asks what the Franks would give for a bag of them, and what the Gotlander at the hornbeam fort gave. He is surprised that you have been so far.
On the island a skipper who brings Botgair his iron says the old man weighs fair and is thought a fool for it. The white silver is under floors here, he says, and not for showing to guests.

You set your own balance on the plank, with weights neither of them poured. Botgair tries it against his. Kantegede tries it against a stone he takes from his belt. Neither says anything for some time.

A Dane you know is at the plank, weighing for another man. He had a guest house and scales of his own at the lake of the Este, until a guest of his robbed a burning. He weighs your silver true and does not use your name.

On the eastern river the woman who speaks for the trappers turns over a lump of amber and asks where it was last offered. The old Gotlander of the Curonian coast sends on what was refused there. She has learned to ask.

Holmfast buys furs on the Curonian shore in a good year and counts Botgair's bundles of forty over again in front of him. Botgair lets him. A man who counts twice has been cheated once, he says, and he would like to know by whom.

endings.how: You brought a balance of your own and let both of them test it, and stood by its reading when it cost you.
endings.text: From that spring the amber is weighed on the Frisian's beam when the Frisian is in. When he is not, each of them weighs on his own and they split the difference, which they call 'the Frisian's share', and nobody collects it.
endings.reward: A standing price at Grobin: amber and squirrel at the better of the two weighings, and no haggling needed; Botgair and Kantegede both friendly; the house is the witness to their bargains (act:witness here pays a small gift each call).

endings.how: You weighed on Botgair's scale and took his number, every time.
endings.text: Botgair is glad of it and gives you first pick of the large pieces. The Curonians bring you nothing directly again: what you buy here you buy through the Gotlander, at the Gotlander's price, for as long as there is a Gotlander.
endings.reward: Botgair as a fast friend and the pick of his store; a tie to his kin on Gotland. After the booths thin, about 813, the house has no friend on the bank and must begin again with the son.

endings.how: You took Kantegede's weighing and paid in iron and salt instead of silver.
endings.text: The go-between says it may be remembered, and it is. His son, grown, knows your boat by its mast and lets it in when other western ships are turned back at the bar.
endings.reward: Entry to the market after 800 without the gift at the gate, inherited by the heir; Curonian amber at source in autumn; Botgair cools, and says only that he hopes you got good weight.

stories.reward: A fixed, fair weighing on a coast that has no coin, with one people or the other or, hardest, both.

stories.title: The old tribute
stories.summary: Eleven Svear on a fort hill still speak of a tribute their grandfathers took, and the Curonians remember that it stopped. Both sides want the same thing from a man off the Franks' river, and it is the one thing his king forbids him to carry. Whoever gets the blades, or whether nobody does, decides how the hill changes hands.
stories.picture: The gap in a log fence on a steep spit at evening: a broad Svea with a square beard and a tall Curonian with a notched staff facing each other across a bundle in sailcloth lying on the ground, the merchant standing behind it, the river and the booths small below.

beats.text: Arnvald asks, away from the others, whether you have iron of the long kind. A sword is worth three times its Rhine price here, he says, and he will pay in pelts by the forty. He has been promised blades before, by a Frisian, through a Dane.

Kantegede walks down to the boat with you, speaking of the weather. At the water he asks what the man on the hill asked, and says that his people would pay in amber, and would pay more. It may be, he says, that you carry nothing of the kind.

Asulf the dealer knows the tale. Thiadbod of Dorestad took pelts on credit for a Svea over the sea and sent no swords. If you carry them instead, he says, you carry Thiadbod's debt with them, and Thiadbod will know who did it.

Buite hears the question you ask, which is who will win. She answers the one you did not ask: that a sword sold to either side will be used, and that one sold to neither will be bought elsewhere, later, from a worse man.
You are on the hill with blades under the ballast and two buyers, and each has a man watching the other's door. Rodlikn says only that she would like to know tonight which benches to make up.

At the kings' mounds the skald tells how the Svear took tribute over the sea, a pelt from every hearth. A man on a hill there sends him a pelt each year to go on telling it. He tells it, and keeps the pelts.
Holmfast carries the messages of the Svea on the Curonian hill home for nothing, and is the only man who brings him an answer. The answer this year is that the king has other uses for ships.

endings.how: You sold the swords to Arnvald.
endings.text: He asks for the tribute at the next thaw, and for two years he gets some of it. In the third the forts inland send men instead of pelts. The Svear go out by boat at night, and the booths under the hill are burnt behind them. Arnvald is laid in the mound field, with a sword.
endings.reward: Pelts at once, three times the Rhine price of the blades; Arnvald's word for the house at Birka and Uppsalir. The Curonians do not forget who armed the hill: after 800 the house pays double at the gate, and Rodlikn's house is gone.

endings.how: You sold the swords to Kantegede.
endings.text: Nothing happens that summer. In the autumn Arnvald counts the spears at the bank, counts his own, and takes a Gotland ship home with his men and his name. The Curonians walk up the hill and shut the gate. Nobody is killed. Botgair stays, as a guest.
endings.reward: Amber, more than the pelts would have fetched; the gate open to the house after 800 with no gift; Rodlikn's house and Botgair's store stand until their deaths. At Birka a few men call the house a seller of the king's shore.

endings.how: You carried no swords here, or carried them past, and told both men so to their faces.
endings.text: Both are angry for a season. The hill changes hands anyway, about the year 800, slowly and with shouting, because eleven men cannot keep it. Buite says the worse man she spoke of never came, and that it surprises her.
endings.reward: No profit, and a clean name on both sides: Arnvald and Kantegede each easy with the house; Buite's answers are free from then on; and no king's man on the Rhine ever has cause to search the boat for what went east.

stories.reward: The hill's goodwill, or the forts', or neither side's blood on the house: and with it how Grobin stands toward the merchant for the next fifty years.

stories.title: Two birds on a stone
stories.summary: In the field of the armed men stands a thin grey stone with two water birds cut on it, of a kind made only on Gotland. Rodlikn's husband's people set it up five generations back, and she wants one cut for herself before the last island woman here is burned. Nobody on this shore can cut it, and nobody on the island remembers the family.
stories.picture: A heath of low mounds under pines: a small upright woman in Gotland brooches with her hand flat on a thin grey slab carved with two duck-like birds facing each other, a merchant crouched to look at the carving, late light coming low between the trees.

beats.text: Rodlikn shows you the stone. Two birds, facing. Nobody knows which birds or why two. Her husband's forefather brought it over the sea in a boat or had it cut here by a man from the island: the family tells it both ways.

She wants one for her own grave, the same size, the same birds. She has the silver: a small bag, weighed twice. What she has not got is a man who cuts stone, or anyone on the island who would know her name.

The wrights on the island's west shore send you to a man who cuts stones for the dead. He cuts ships and riders now, he says: nobody has asked for birds since his grandfather's day. He will do it if you can draw them for him.
Back at the old stone with a strip of birch bark and a burnt stick. Beornwine, who had letters beaten into him at Gyrwe, takes the stick out of your hand and draws the birds himself.

The stone-cutter looks at the birch bark for a long time. Nobody has asked for birds since his grandfather's day; he cuts ships and riders. But he can cut what is drawn. Up the stream, he says, there is a farm whose name she will know.
A slab of island limestone as long as a child lies on the bottom boards, wrapped in a fleece. Tulegaud looks at how the boat sits, looks at the bar, and laughs. Then he goes to fetch men with ropes.

endings.how: You had the stone cut on Gotland and carried it over the bar to her.
endings.text: She stands it by the door of the long house, where she can see it, and says it is to go with her when the time comes. It does, in 818. The house passes to a Curonian girl she had taken in, who keeps your bench and does not know why it is turned to the wall.
endings.reward: Rodlikn as a fast friend for life: lodging, ale and healing free at her house; her account of every Gotland family that trades east, which opens doors at Paviken; and the bench is kept for the heir by the girl after her.

endings.how: You carried the stone, and also found her mother's kin on the island and brought word of them back.
endings.text: A farm on the west shore remembers a daughter who went over the sea six mothers ago. They send a brooch. Rodlikn wears it one summer and then takes the next ship to the island, to die there. The stone stays here, on nobody's grave.
endings.reward: A Gotland farm that counts this house as kin by service: a winter berth and a fair price at Paviken, inherited. Rodlikn's house at Grobin closes when she sails, and Botgair says you have cost him his supper.

endings.how: You took her silver and did not bring the stone, or were wrecked with it, or never went.
endings.text: She does not speak of it. When she is burned in 818 her brooches go with her and nothing marks the place but greener grass. If you were wrecked and told her so, she pours you a cup. If you were not, there is no bench.
endings.reward: Her bag of silver, weighed twice, about 60 d. An honest wreck costs nothing more. A lie costs the house its lodging here and Tulegaud's free pilotage, since he heard it from her.

stories.reward: A house on a far shore where a bench is kept for you and turned to the wall when you leave.

stories.title: The gods who would not answer
stories.summary: About 853 the Cori break a Danish fleet; at Birka the young men say they will do what the Danes could not. A merchant who trades on both shores knows the Svear are coming before the Curonians do, and afterwards hears from a man who was there how an army five days from its ships cast lots and found no god willing to help it.
stories.picture: Night before a timber fort on a hill inland: armed men in a ring round a cloak spread on the ground with cut twigs lying on it, faces turned away from what the twigs say, and at the edge of the firelight three merchants talking low, one with a small cross at his neck.

beats.text: The market is full of Danish things: ring money, a gilt cup with a cross on its foot, ships for sale on the lake shore. Wissegerde says the five towns met the Danes together and killed half. He is selling the gold fast, as if it were fish.

Vigfast says it quietly. The king is gathering ships. The young men want it said that the Svear did what the Danes could not. He names the first town they will come to, and it is the one you sleep in.

You stand at the gate with what you know. Wissegerde has feared those sails all his life. He may believe you, or he may ask why a guest of the Svear is telling him so. On the bank are a few households who could be over the bar in one tide.
From the sea, smoke stands over the pines behind the dunes, a great deal of it. No boat lies at the outlet. The pilot's pole is stuck upright in the sand.

Vigfast tells it: the town burnt, five days' march, eight days before a second fort, the lots cast and no god willing. Then the merchants said to ask Christ, and it fell well. He has eaten no meat for forty days.
The priest at the harbour church has the story already, from the bishop's own people, and tells it as a victory. He asks what you saw. What you saw was smoke.

At the lake of the Este the news comes by the amber boats: the hornbeam fort is burnt, and the Svear went on five days inland. The fort on the rise doubles its watch. The amber-cutters say the Cori's prices were false anyway.

On Gotland nobody is surprised. No Gotlander has been buried on that shore for a lifetime, they say, and whoever still kept a booth there had been told. They ask what became of the Danes' ships that lay for sale on that lake shore.

endings.how: You told Wissegerde what was coming, and were believed.
endings.text: The Svear burn an emptied town. The people are inland, behind the second fort's fence, and are among those who buy their lives there at half a pound of silver a man. Wissegerde lives. He never thanks you: he sends amber to your house every autumn until he dies.
endings.reward: A sack of amber each autumn while Wissegerde lives, brought to any port the house names on this sea; the Curonians' good word, which opens their coast to the house by truce in the years after; at Birka, if it is known, a hard season.

endings.how: You said nothing at the gate, and took whoever would come from the bank over the bar in your own boat.
endings.text: Eleven people and a loom, in a boat built for four men. Tulegaud walks ahead of you in the water to his chest. You set them down on Gotland or at the lake of the Este. The town burns behind you with its fighting men in it.
endings.reward: Those you carried and their kin as friends for good, wherever they were set down: a house on Gotland or at Truso that lodges yours; the pilot's son as a pilot for the house on any Baltic shore (the same knowledge as unlock_pilot_curonia). No silver at all.

endings.how: You sailed with the king's ships as a victualler, as some merchants did.
endings.text: You see the town burnt from the lake, and you are among those at the second fort when the lots fall badly and the merchants speak up. You are paid in Danish gold that has now changed hands twice. Vigfast will sit with you. No Curonian will, in your lifetime or your heir's.
endings.reward: About 400 d in gold and silver for the season's stores; the text of the lots (Rimbert c. 30, Robinson 1921: texts_more.json rimbert_lots_in_courland) heard at first hand; the king's men at Birka friendly. The Curonian coast is shut to the house until the next generation.

endings.how: You heard the warning at Birka and kept off this coast for the year.
endings.text: You hear the rest at Birka from Vigfast, and at Sliesthorp from the priest, and the two accounts do not agree about whose victory it was. Nobody at Grobin knows that you knew.
endings.reward: Vigfast's account, and with it a rumour worth silver in the west: which coast is burnt, where Danish gold is cheap, and that amber will be dear at Truso for two years.

stories.reward: People alive who would not have been, or the king's gold, or only the knowledge: the merchant chooses which of his two shores he keeps.

works.name: Withies in the outlet
works.what: Each spring after the ice, peeled willow stakes are driven along both sides of wherever the water now runs out over the bar, with a wisp of straw tied to the seaward pair. A storm will take them, and they are set again.
works.needs: Tulegaud at least easy with you, and a call in spring, since last year's stakes mark last year's channel.
works.gives: For that sailing season the house crosses the bar without waiting for the pilot and with small risk of grounding; other skippers use the stakes too, and the pilot tells them whose silver set them.
works.picture: A man to his waist in brown water driving a peeled stake with a wooden maul, a line of pale stakes behind him leading out through broken surf, a small boat waiting with more stakes across her thwarts.
works.source: invented in the period's manner: marking a shifting channel with stakes is the ordinary practice of shallow coasts (?). The outlet silted and moved until 1697-1703 (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md). No such marks are recorded here, and they are not a landmark: they last a season.

works.name: A hard of logs on the bank
works.what: Split alder logs laid side by side across the mud of the landing and pegged down, wide enough for one boat, with two rollers kept beside it. A boat can be drawn up dry-shod and loaded without sinking to the knee.
works.needs: Leave from whoever holds the bank that year: Botgair until about 812, the Curonians' man after.
works.gives: Loading and unloading here take half the time; careening and repair cost less; the place on the bank is the house's own, and is kept free for it.
works.picture: A river bank of dark mud under a fort hill, a strip of pale new logs running from the water up to the booths, a small clinker boat drawn half onto it on rollers, men carrying sacks dry-footed.
works.source: invented in the period's manner: no jetty or landing stage has been reported at Grobiņa (dossier 1, 2), so this is a log hard, not a quay. Log trackways on wet ground are common in the Baltic lands (?).

works.name: A bay in the locked store
works.what: A partition of split planks in the Gotlanders' store with its own shelf, hooks in the rafters for pelts, and a tally stick with your house's mark hung beside Botgair's.
works.needs: Botgair, or after him Wissegerde, friendly with you.
works.gives: Goods can lie here over a winter: amber bought cheap after the gales waits for the spring ship, and furs bought at the thaw are safe from mice and damp. One bay, about a small boat's load.
works.picture: The inside of a dark log store: sacks, hanging pelts, a new partition of pale planks, and two notched tally sticks on one peg by the door post, an old one and a new one.
works.source: invented in the period's manner; no storehouse is reported (dossier 2). The cheap and dear months of amber are goods_793.json's (cheap in months 10 to 12, dear in 6 to 8).

works.name: A mound in the field of the armed men
works.what: A pyre, and then a low round mound of sand and turf over what is left, seven paces across and knee high like the others, for a man of your crew who died on this coast or for a friend here who has no kin left to raise one.
works.needs: A death: a crewman's on this shore, or Arnvald's or Botgair's. Wood, hands, ale for those who dig, and something of the dead man's to go in.
works.gives: The dead man is remembered here (act:remember at the mounds); the crew's heart is steadier for it; the Northmen of the place count the house as one that buries its own, and say so at Birka and on Gotland.
works.picture: A bare new mound of pale sand among hundreds of old heather-grown ones under pines, a burnt patch beside it, four men leaning on wooden spades and a woman pouring from a cup.
works.source: The Priediens mounds: mostly 7 to 10 m across and 0.5 m high, cremations (lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis'). A Christian crewman would want earth and a priest and can have neither here: the nearest church is across the sea.

ships.how: built to order over a winter, or bought second-hand in spring
ships.note: The boat of this shore: broad, shallow, about ten metres, light enough to drag over a sand bar. On the boat bank they are riveted in the Northmen's way, not pegged like the Wends'. She crosses the bar laden where a deeper ship must lighten. About 500 d (unlocks_793.json).
ships.picture: A broad shallow clinker boat half planked on blocks on a river bank deep in wood chips, a tar pot smoking on a tripod beside her, a fort hill behind.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json baltic_coastal_boat ('riveted boats at Truso and Grobina'); story/ships_793.json built_at truso, grobin; unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_baltic_coastal_boat (500 d, to 850; the price is a guess (?))

ships.how: bought from the Curonians on the lake
ships.note: A hollowed trunk for the lake and the river: one man or two, a paddle, a pole. Useless at sea and the only thing that will go everywhere on the reed lake. Cheap, and paid for in iron sooner than silver.
ships.picture: A dark hollowed log with a man standing in it poling through reeds, eel traps stacked in the bow, flat grey water all round.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json logboat; peoples/baltic_east.md 6 (Balts: logboat, baltic_coastal_boat). No boat has been found at Grobiņa in what was opened (?).

ships.how: bought second-hand from a Gotland household
ships.note: A light clinker boat of the island kind, four or five pairs of oars, kept by the Gotland households for the lake and for meeting ships at the bar. As the households thin there is a boat more than there are rowers, and Botgair sells one.
ships.picture: A slim tarred rowing boat drawn up among logboats on a muddy bank, oars laid inside, a lean man with a plaited beard resting one hand on her stem.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_small_boat. That the Gotlanders here kept such boats is inferred from their being islanders trading over a lake, not found (?).

sayings.text: We desire peace rather than fighting, and we wish to enter into an agreement with you.
sayings.source: The Cori to the Svear at Apulia, about 854: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii c. 30 (tr. C. H. Robinson, 1921). Said here after 854 of any hard bargain, by Curonians, drily.

sayings.text: Having cast lots they failed to discover any god who was willing to aid them.
sayings.source: Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921), of the Svear before Apulia. Vigfast says it of a bad season's trade, and then looks over his shoulder.

sayings.text: To win for themselves the reputation that they could do what the Danes had not done.
sayings.source: Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921): why the Svear sailed. The oldest reason on this sea, and Botgair's whole opinion of young men.

sayings.text: Crooked and far is the road to a foe, / Though his house on the highway be; / But wide and straight is the way to a friend, / Though far away he fare.
sayings.source: Hávamál 34, tr. Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (1923) (lore/proverbs_jokes.json pj008). Rodlikn's, for a crew that came back over the bar.

sayings.text: He welcomes the night whose fare is enough, / (Short are the yards of a ship,) / Uneasy are autumn nights; / Full oft does the weather change in a week, / And more in a month's time.
sayings.source: Hávamál 74, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj145). Said on the bank in the amber season, when every skipper is counting days to the ice.

sayings.text: Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest / In a single spot forever; / Love becomes loathing if long one sits / By the hearth in another's home.
sayings.source: Hávamál 35, tr. Bellows 1923 (proverbs_jokes.json pj009). After 800 the Curonians could say it of five generations of Northmen; a Gotlander says it first, to save them the trouble.

sayings.text: Last year's channel drowns this year's fool.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the pilot's; the outlet shifted every winter)

sayings.text: The Danes brought us gold and the Svear came to fetch it. We only kept it warm.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner, on Rimbert c. 30: the gold taken from the Danes about 853 is paid to the Svear about 854. A Curonian's understatement, after the war.

sayings.text: Eleven men hold the hill. Ten, when one goes for ale.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (a Gotlander on the Svear at the gate, before 800)

easter_eggs.text: The thin grey stone with two duck-like birds is 0.70 m high and a hand's breadth thick. Stones of its kind are otherwise found only on Gotland. It will be dug out of a grave in this field in 1987, and nobody will know then, either, which birds they are.
easter_eggs.source: en.wikipedia 'Grobiņa'; lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis' (0.70 m high, 0.08 m thick, second half of the 7th century, found at Priediens in 1987). That it stood in the open in 793 is the game's guess (?).

easter_eggs.text: Nobody in the market calls this place by the name on your chart. A Saxon monk will write it down about 870 as Seeburg, the fort by the lake, or by the sea: he had it from Svear, and it is their word, not the Curonians'. The name Grobin is not written until 1253.
easter_eggs.source: Rimbert c. 30 (Robinson 1921); lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' and 'Grobiņas pilskalns' (first written 1253; rendered Jūrpils or Ezerpils); dossier 1. Robinson's own note of 1921 put Seeburg on the Düna: the match with this place came with the digs of 1929.

easter_eggs.text: Ask Buite what the hornbeams by the women's ground are for and she says: for shade. The town's later name may come from a Curonian word for a hornbeam wood.
easter_eggs.source: lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' (gruobīns; the fort hill is Skābarža kalns, 'hornbeam hill'); the meaning is from memory (?); dossier 1

easter_eggs.text: Count the mounds and you get a different number each time. So will everyone after you: two thousand by one count, one thousand by another, four hundred and fifty left standing.
easter_eggs.source: lv.wikipedia 'Grobiņas arheoloģiskais ansamblis' (about 2,000); sv.wikipedia 'Grobiņa' (about 450 left of about 1,000); dossier 2, 8

easter_eggs.text: If you robbed the heaps at the burning by the lake of the Este, the Dane who answered for you is here, weighing amber on another man's scale. He weighs your silver true to the grain and never once uses your name.
easter_eggs.source: the chain amber_road, ending end_shut (writing/chain_amber_road.json chain_amber_road.end_shut.host_paid: 'He is at Grobin now, weighing for another man'); shown only with flag ch_amber_road_end_shut

easter_eggs.text: A saga written four hundred years on tells of a Northman on this coast who was taken at a farm, broke loose at night with the farmer's silver, and went back to say who had robbed him, since leaving unseen would be a thief's act. After 855 an old Curonian tells a tale very like it, and in his telling the Northman is the fool.
easter_eggs.source: Egil's saga c. 46 (13th century; LATER; from memory (?)); en.wikipedia 'Courland'; dossier 3, 7. The Curonian's version is invented.

unlocks.what: A bench kept at Rodlikn's long house, turned to the wall when you leave
unlocks.how: Sleep there on three calls and pay what is owed; made lasting by ending 'Two birds on a stone' with the stone brought.
unlocks.gives: Free lodging and a cup for the crew at Grobin (lodge, drink); Rodlikn's rumours each call; morale holds over a wait for wind here. Kept for the heir by the girl who has the house after 818.

unlocks.what: The house's balance is the one both peoples weigh by
unlocks.how: End 'Weighed twice' by standing to your own scale's reading before both Botgair and Kantegede (needs the thread's flag sv_scale).
unlocks.gives: Amber and squirrel here at the better of the two weighings without haggling; a small gift each time the house witnesses a bargain (act:witness); both men friendly.

unlocks.what: Tulegaud takes the house over the bar unasked and unpaid
unlocks.how: Lodge at Rodlikn's and do what he says on three crossings; or pay for the withies in the outlet twice.
unlocks.gives: No pilot's fee and no wait at the bar while he lives, and his son's after him; the same knowledge the amber road chain gives as unlock_pilot_curonia, reached another way.

unlocks.what: Entry to the Curonians' market after 800 without the gift at the gate
unlocks.how: End 'The old tribute' with the blades to the forts, or 'Weighed twice' as the Curonians' guest.
unlocks.gives: The house's truce here is not counted in days; Curonian amber at source in autumn (buy_at_source); inherited by the heir at half strength, as feeling is.

unlocks.what: A sack of amber sent to the house each autumn
unlocks.how: End 'The gods who would not answer' by warning the fort, about 854.
unlocks.gives: One sack of amber each autumn at a port of this sea the house names, while Wissegerde lives (goods amber); and the Curonian coast open to the house by truce after the burning.
